summary:
The Melody of Water (developed for the Earth Jukebox challenge) is an immersive web platform designed to make global river data accessible through interactive sound. It sonifies real satellite hydrology datasets from NASA’s SWOT mission and Earth Information Center visualizations (including major rivers such as the Amazon, Paraná, and Mississippi, among others).
Designed with visually impaired users in mind, the interface replaces visual-only maps with voice commands, hand-tracking, and gesture controls. As users move their hand across a river, spatial audio adjusting volume based on proximity guides them along the channel. Using hand gestures, users isolate and combine different hydrological variables (such as channel width, water level, slope, and seasonal/temporal amplitude), each mapped to different orchestral instruments to generate distinct melodies from the same river.
By transforming complex Earth observation data into an intuitive musical experience, the project provides key tools to improve accessibility empowering non-visual users to independently explore and understand the planet's major waterways. While this demo focuses on rivers, the underlying concept is adaptable to many other types of geographic data.
details:
The project is a web application hosted on GitHub Pages that offers an interactive experience designed to convey visual and geographic information about the world's rivers through music. The entire platform is controlled by voice commands using the speech-to-text Web Speech API to navigate the menus, which was chosen because it requires no backend processing. At the same time, it integrates the text-to-speech model Edge TTS, allowing users to explore the site in a completely non-visual way.

Each river, displayed on an interactive screen map, generates a unique musical piece based on its physical characteristics across different segments: amplitude is represented by double basses and horns, channel width by woodwinds, water level by strings, and slope by harps and timpani. Combining all these instruments creates a dynamic orchestra where the user acts as the conductor.

Using hand tracking through a webcam powered by MediaPipe, the entire interaction is driven by hand movements and gestures. The right hand moves a point across the screen that acts as the sound focus; as it gets closer to the river, the volume increases, and as it moves away, the sound fades. Furthermore, each finger is assigned to a specific physical characteristic, so lowering a finger mutes its corresponding instrument, allowing the user to isolate the exact data layers they want to hear. Finally, making a fist with the left hand and rotating it counterclockwise rewinds time to switch through the seasons of the year, enabling the analysis of different temporal datasets for the same river.

The primary datasets come from the Earth Information Center, but since that source only covered five rivers, we accessed the underlying satellite measurements from the SWOT mission (by NASA and CNES) and used the Hydrocron API to extract data for additional waterways.
dataRefs: SWOT Mission Unlocks a New View of Our Waterways
